segments.text: Juvenile delinquency concerns unlawful or problematic conduct by persons legally treated as juveniles.

Legal definitions depend on age and statute; behavioural definitions may be broader. A status offence is conduct prohibited because of the person’s juvenile status, whereas delinquent acts may correspond to offences more generally.

Juvenile delinquency can mean legally prohibited conduct committed by a person below the age threshold defined by juvenile law. Behavioural research may use the term more broadly for persistent antisocial or rule-breaking conduct. A legal definition must always follow the jurisdiction’s statute because age thresholds and procedures vary.

A status offence is conduct prohibited because of the young person’s age but not criminal for an adult, such as certain truancy or curfew violations in jurisdictions that recognize such categories. It should not be confused with an ordinary criminal offence committed by a child.

Research commonly examines family conflict, weak supervision, school exclusion, peer influence, neighbourhood disadvantage, substance use, trauma, impulsivity and opportunity. These are risk factors, not destiny. Protective factors—including supportive adults, education, stable routines and prosocial peers—can reduce risk and support desistance.

Development matters because adolescence involves changing impulse control, sensitivity to peers and identity formation. This helps explain why juvenile systems emphasize proportionality, diversion and rehabilitation more strongly than purely punitive models.

Official statistics reflect offences detected and recorded by institutions; victimization data reflect experiences reported by victims; self-report studies capture some behaviour never detected by police. None is a complete measure. Arrest or case figures may change because of policing practice even if underlying behaviour remains stable.
Whenever using a statistic, state the jurisdiction, age group, reference year and whether the figure concerns arrests, accused persons, convictions or self-reported conduct.

items.text: Juvenile delinquency is defined partly by law because the legal age and special juvenile status determine who enters the juvenile justice system.
Behavioural definitions may include troublesome or risky conduct wider than criminal offences, while legal definitions focus on conduct and age categories recognized by law.

Status offences are important conceptually because the behaviour is prohibited or specially regulated because the actor is a child or young person; the same conduct may not be an offence for an adult.

Official statistics record cases known to or processed by authorities. They can reveal patterns but may understate actual offending because many incidents are not reported, detected or formally recorded.

rows: Common confusion to avoid: Do not quote an age limit or juvenile-crime statistic without checking the current Pakistani law and the year/source of the data.

items.text: Use current juvenile-justice law for age and legal procedure.

segments.text: Juvenile justice emphasizes age and developmental status.
Official statistics show recorded cases, not necessarily the full amount of offending.
